title: From generation to generation
hookLine: the phrase that ends the Kedushah

cards: Partway through a weekday service, the leader repeats the standing prayer, the Amidah, out loud, and the room changes. Leader and congregation start trading lines from the Bible, back and forth, a call and an answer.
Some people rise up onto their toes. First comes Isaiah's vision of the angels: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". Then Ezekiel's: blessed be the glory of the LORD from His place.
Then a verse from the Psalms. And just before the closing hallelujah, the congregation sings today's word.

teach.b: L'dor vador. Dor means generation. L'dor, to a generation; vador, and a generation: from generation to generation.
That section of the service is the Kedushah, the prayer of holiness, and its last verse is from Psalm 146: the LORD will reign for ever, your God, O Zion, l'dor vador, hallelujah.
Then, in the Ashkenazi wording, the leader picks the phrase straight back up: l'dor vador nagid godlecha, from generation to generation we will tell of your greatness. Look at the shape of it.

Isaiah's angels call holy in heaven. Ezekiel hears the glory moving from its place. Then the prayer comes down to earth and lands on something very human: parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren.
Holiness here isn't only sung. It's handed down. The phrase has roots in the Torah too.

teach.h: THIS IS MY MEMORIAL UNTO ALL GENERATIONS.
teach.b: At the burning bush, God gives Moses a name and says, "this is My memorial unto all generations", in Hebrew, l'dor dor.
A memorial keeps memory alive, so the zachor of a few days ago and today's phrase belong together: remembering is how anything gets from one generation to another. And the Kedushah is a conversation.
The congregation answers the leader; the leader answers the congregation. Passing something on works like that too. The young don't only receive.
They answer back, with questions and new melodies of their own, and the answer becomes part of what the next generation hears.

how: When a minyan is present, the leader repeats the Amidah aloud and the congregation joins in the Kedushah, standing; in the Ashkenazi wording the leader then continues with l'dor vador nagid godlecha.

o: a blessing said over a newborn child

p: we will tell of your greatness

s: l'dor vador means from generation to generation

games.q: you're leading the service. the congregation has just sung the psalm's last words, l'dor vador. in the Ashkenazi wording, what do you sing next?
o: amen, and the prayer is over.
l'dor vador nagid godlecha: from generation to generation we will tell of your greatness.
holy, holy, holy, one more time.
games.why: the leader picks the congregation's last words straight back up: from generation to generation we will tell of your greatness. a call, then an answer, then a promise to keep telling.

practice: Bring to mind someone younger than you, a child, a niece or nephew, a student, a new coworker, a neighbor's kid, and hold their face for a moment.
Ask two things: what do I know that they might need someday, and what do they know that I don't? If you pray, say the psalm's two words quietly, l'dor vador; if you don't, just hold their name.

wordCard.voice: L'dor vador. From generation to generation: the words near the end of the Kedushah, from Psalm 146. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: to a generation and a generation, from generation to generation.

carryVoice: Your line: generation to generation. A call, an answer, and then the next voice. Back tomorrow, same hill.
